REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH DECISIONMAKING DISCRIMINATION PROTECTION (FEHA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California law on "reproductive health decisionmaking" as a protected characteristic under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). It is provided to Jordan Lee by Acme, Inc. It states facts about what the relevant statutes say and about what one California Court of Appeal decision has said about this characteristic's scope and history. It does not evaluate, and takes no position on, any specific employment decision, request, or dispute involving Jordan Lee or any other person.

WHAT "REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH DECISIONMAKING" MEANS UNDER FEHA
California Government Code § 12926(y) defines "reproductive health decisionmaking" for purposes of the FEHA. The definition is expressly non-exhaustive: it "includes, but is not limited to," a decision to use or access a particular drug, device, product, or medical service for reproductive health. The same subdivision also clarifies that listing "reproductive health decisionmaking" as its own characteristic does not mean the FEHA's separate definition of "sex" — which independently includes pregnancy and pregnancy-related medical conditions — excludes reproductive health decisionmaking; the two categories can overlap.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "“Reproductive health decisionmaking” includes, but is not limited to, a decision to use or access a particular drug, device, product, or medical service for reproductive health. This subdivision and other provisions in this part relating to “reproductive health decisionmaking” shall not be construed to mean that subdivision (r) of this section and other provisions in this part related to “sex” do not include reproductive health decisionmaking."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12926(y) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  Known gap: This definition is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to"), and no published California appellate decision located in this research construes where its outer boundary lies — for example, whether a decision about a medical service that is not itself contraception, fertility treatment, abortion, or a similarly reproductive-health-specific service would still qualify. This clause quotes the current text of § 12926(y), which was itself most recently amended effective January 1, 2026; this document does not track or compare any earlier version of the subdivision's wording, and does not address whether that 2026 amendment changed the definition's substance or only its surrounding subdivisions.

THE PROHIBITION: REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH DECISIONMAKING AS A LISTED PROTECTED CHARACTERISTIC
California Government Code § 12940(a) makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to hire or employ a person, to refuse to select a person for a training program leading to employment, to bar or discharge a person from employment or from such a training program, or to discriminate against a person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of that person's reproductive health decisionmaking. The same sentence lists reproductive health decisionmaking alongside race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, and veteran or military status.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "For an employer, because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status of any person, to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12940(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the opening sentence of subdivision (a); it does not address FEHA's separate harassment prohibition (§ 12940(j)) or retaliation prohibition (§ 12940(h)), each of which uses different statutory language that was not independently fetched or verified for this document. It also does not address § 12940's own introductory qualifiers — a bona fide-occupational-qualification exception and an exception for conduct based on applicable federal or California security regulations, both stated in the statute's chapeau rather than in subdivision (a) itself — so this document does not resolve whether either exception could apply to any particular reproductive-health-decisionmaking-based employment action.

WHICH EMPLOYERS THIS PROHIBITION REACHES
For purposes of this prohibition, California Government Code § 12926(d) defines "employer" to include any person regularly employing five or more persons, as well as any person acting as an agent of an employer, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities. The statute then carves out a specific exception to that definition: it does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "“Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, except as follows:"
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12926(d), first sentence (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  "“Employer” does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12926(d), second sentence (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  Known gap: This document does not evaluate whether any specific religious or nonprofit entity qualifies for the statutory exception. It also does not verify whether FEHA provisions outside this general Article 1 employer definition — for instance, provisions elsewhere in § 12940 that by their own terms may apply without regard to employee count — use a different threshold; only this general employer definition was fetched and confirmed for this document. Independent-contractor status, joint-employer questions, and staffing-agency or franchise arrangements are also not addressed.

WHEN AND HOW THIS PROTECTION WAS ADDED
A California Court of Appeal decision states that reproductive health decisionmaking protection was added to the FEHA through Senate Bill No. 523 (2021-2022 Regular Session), effective January 1, 2023. A separate, later Court of Appeal decision — issued in a different, non-employment context — independently describes the same statutory definition as having been added by "the Contraceptive Equity Act of 2022," and identifies the specific chaptered-law citation for that enactment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The statute has since been amended to include protection for “reproductive health decisionmaking.” (See § 12940, subd. (a), as amended through Sen. Bill No. 523 (2021-2022 Reg. Sess.), effective Jan. 1, 2023.)"
  — Paleny v. Fireplace Products U.S., Inc. (Cal. Ct. App., Third Dist., filed June 27, 2024, certified for publication), footnote 3, California Court of Appeal, Third Appellate District (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9965196/paleny-v-fireplace-products-us-inc/)
  "The term was added by the Contraceptive Equity Act of 2022 (see Stats. 2022, ch. 630, §§ 3–5) and is defined as follows:"
  — Tulare Medical Center Property etc. v. Valdivia (Cal. Ct. App., filed Apr. 8, 2026, published), California Court of Appeal (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10839263/tulare-medical-center-property-etc-v-valdivia/)
  Known gap: The second citation below comes from a Court of Appeal opinion analyzing the Unruh Civil Rights Act's incorporation of FEHA definitions in a public-accommodations dispute, not an employment case; it is quoted here only for its description of this definition's legislative history, not for any employment-law holding, and this document does not otherwise rely on or summarize that case's substantive ruling. Neither citation below is to the enacted bill text, the Legislative Counsel's Digest, or the Secretary of State's chaptered-statute record itself — this document did not independently fetch or verify those primary sources, and instead relies on these two appellate descriptions of them, which corroborate each other on the year of enactment (2022 session) but describe the underlying act by two different names ("Senate Bill No. 523" and "the Contraceptive Equity Act of 2022").

WHAT ONE COURT DID NOT DECIDE: RETROACTIVITY AND THE PRE-AMENDMENT FRAMEWORK
In the same decision cited above, the employee raised the reproductive-health-decisionmaking amendment on appeal after her employment had already ended and after the trial court had already ruled against her. The Court of Appeal did not decide whether the amendment applies to conduct that occurred before its effective date; it found that the employee had forfeited any argument about retroactive application by not raising it in her opening brief. Applying the pre-amendment framework instead, the same court held that the employee — who had undergone an elective egg-retrieval and freezing procedure without an underlying medical condition related to pregnancy — did not have a protected characteristic under the FEHA as it existed before the amendment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Appellant also does not address the retroactivity of this amendment other than to assert, in her reply brief, as she did at oral argument, that the amendment was a mere clarification of existing law, i.e., the forms of sex discrimination, and thus presents no question of retroactivity. As we have indicated, the issue of retroactivity was not addressed in her opening brief, and we thus find it forfeited."
  — Paleny v. Fireplace Products U.S., Inc. (Cal. Ct. App., Third Dist., filed June 27, 2024, certified for publication), California Court of Appeal, Third Appellate District (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9965196/paleny-v-fireplace-products-us-inc/)
  "Again, there is no evidence that appellant was pregnant, infertile, or addressing some other medical condition. She was undergoing an elective medical procedure but, without an underlying medical condition related to pregnancy, appellant does not have a protected characteristic under the FEHA."
  — Paleny v. Fireplace Products U.S., Inc. (Cal. Ct. App., Third Dist., filed June 27, 2024, certified for publication), California Court of Appeal, Third Appellate District (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9965196/paleny-v-fireplace-products-us-inc/)
  Known gap: Both quotations in this clause are to the same appellate decision as the enactment-history clause above, not to independent corroborating sources. Because the retroactivity question was resolved on forfeiture rather than on the merits, no appellate authority located in this research decides whether reproductive-health-decisionmaking protection reaches conduct that predates January 1, 2023. Separately, because the amendment did not apply to the case, the court's holding that an elective procedure without an underlying medical condition was unprotected was reached under the pre-amendment "sex"/pregnancy framework only — this document does not determine, and no case found in this research resolves, whether the same or similar facts would come out differently today under the current, amended definition of reproductive health decisionmaking.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge that you have received and read this document.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Company: Acme, Inc.
Date: September 8, 2026
City, State: Oakland, California
